chunks: As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, from Fadalah, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'ab, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:
Ali عليه السلام did not deem ghusl obligatory for anything except upon the major fluid.

The correct way to understand this report is that when the two circumcised parts do not meet, ghusl is not obligatory except with the major fluid, because a man may see in sleep that he had intercourse, then when he awakens he sees nothing; so ghusl is not obligatory upon him unless he awakens and sees the fluid. This indicates that it is specific to this situation.

key_terms.الْخِتَانَانِ: the two circumcised parts, referring to the sexual organs of the spouses
key_terms.الْغُسْلَ: ritual bath that becomes obligatory in specific states of major ritual impurity
key_terms.الْمَاءِ الْأَكْبَرِ: the major fluid that necessitates ghusl
key_terms.مَخْصُوصٌ: restricted or specified to a particular circumstance

ai.seo_question: When does ghusl become obligatory if there was no actual contact of the two circumcised parts?
ai.summary: This report discusses a fiqh ruling concerning when ghusl becomes obligatory. It explains that in the absence of the meeting of the two circumcised parts, ghusl is only required if the major fluid is seen, such as after a dream when one awakens and finds discharge.
